title: SHOULD MARRIED PEOPLE KEEP THEIR EXES ON SOCIAL MEDIA? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHETHER YOU STILL LOVE THEM—IT’S WHY YOU STILL NEED THE DOOR OPEN
paragraphs: SHOULD MARRIED PEOPLE KEEP THEIR EXES ON SOCIAL MEDIA? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHETHER YOU STILL LOVE THEM—IT’S WHY YOU STILL NEED THE DOOR OPEN
That “harmless” follow may mean absolutely nothing. But if protecting it matters more to you than protecting your spouse’s heart, something deeper may already be happening.
It’s only a follow.
That’s what you tell yourself.
You don’t message them.
You’re not cheating.
You don’t meet secretly.
You’re married now. You love your spouse. That relationship ended years ago.
So why should it matter that your ex can still see your life?
Why should it matter that you can still see theirs?
Then one night, while your spouse is sleeping beside you, you’re scrolling.
And there they are.
Your ex.
Older now.
Different.
Maybe married.
Maybe single.
Maybe smiling beside someone else.
You don’t touch the message button.
You barely pause.
But something inside you does.
And sometimes the most dangerous doors are not the ones we walk through.
They are the ones we insist on keeping unlocked.
So let’s deal with this carefully, because Christians can make two opposite mistakes here.
One is pretending boundaries do not matter.
The other is inventing commandments God never gave.
The Bible does not say, “Thou shalt unfriend your ex.”
There is no verse commanding every married Christian to remove every former boyfriend, girlfriend, fiancé, or romantic interest from every social-media platform.
We must be honest about that.
Following an ex is not automatically adultery.
Being followed by an ex is not automatically emotional unfaithfulness.
Some people may have legitimate reasons for limited contact, especially when children, family responsibilities, work, ministry, or unavoidable community connections are involved.
But biblical wisdom asks a deeper question than:
“Am I technically allowed to do this?”
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:23:
The Christian life is not merely about discovering how close we can stand to a cliff without falling.
It is about asking what glorifies Christ.
What builds others up.
What protects what God has entrusted to us.
What makes love stronger rather than merely proving that something is technically permissible.
And marriage changes the question.
Because once you have entered a marriage covenant, the issue is no longer simply:
“Do I have feelings for my ex?”
A more mature question is:
“Does keeping this connection help me love my spouse faithfully, transparently, sacrificially, and securely before Christ?”
There is a line in Proverbs that becomes painfully relevant here.
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mikkol-mishmar netzor libbekha.
“Guard your heart with all diligence…”
Proverbs 4:23.
The Hebrew verb נְצֹר (netzor) carries the sense of guarding, watching, preserving.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
“Trust your heart.”
It says guard it.
Why?
Because human hearts drift.
Memories romanticize.
Loneliness exaggerates.
Disappointment rewrites history.
And social media has given previous relationships something earlier generations rarely possessed:
persistent visibility.
Once, someone could leave your life.
Today, they can remain in your pocket.
Their birthday.
Their vacation.
Their marriage.
Their divorce.
Their new haircut.
Their heartbreak.
Their late-night story.
Their “remember this?” photograph.
Their message notification.
Their name appearing when your marriage is going through its worst month.
That does not mean everyone will fall into sin.
Sometimes it arrives disguised as nostalgia.
Sometimes curiosity.
Sometimes closure.
Sometimes concern.
Sometimes, “I was just checking how they were doing.”
Sometimes, “We’re only friends.”
And sometimes that is genuinely true.
But sometimes “friendship” becomes the respectable word we use because we are uncomfortable admitting that a tiny part of us enjoys knowing the door is still there.
That is where this article stops being about your ex.
Because perhaps the real question is not:
“Should married people keep exes on social media?”
Perhaps the real question is:
“Why do I need to?”
That question can hurt.
Especially when the answer underneath it is something we never intended to say aloud.
Maybe you enjoy being remembered.
Maybe you like knowing they still watch your stories.
Maybe their likes still give you something.
Maybe you occasionally wonder what life would have been like.
Maybe nothing inappropriate has happened—but you know you would feel uncomfortable if your spouse saw every interaction.
Maybe you compare.
Maybe when your marriage becomes difficult, memories of your ex become strangely selective.
You remember the laughter but forget the dysfunction.
You remember the chemistry but forget why it ended.
You remember being wanted but forget being wounded.

You compare somebody else’s carefully edited social-media presence with the exhausted human being sleeping beside you—the person who pays bills with you, raises children with you, sees your worst moods, knows your weaknesses, carries burdens with you, and has to love the version of you that never appears in photographs.
That comparison is brutally unfair.
Your ex gets remembered in highlights.
Your spouse has to live with the behind-the-scenes footage.
And suddenly yesterday begins competing with the covenant God has placed in your hands today.
This is why boundaries are not automatically insecurity.
Sometimes boundaries are love wearing work clothes.
Paul gives husbands an astonishing standard in Ephesians 5:25:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Look at those words.
ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate.
Love.
παρέδωκεν — paredōken.
Gave Himself up.
Christian marital love is therefore not built around:
“What am I entitled to keep?”
Its model is Christ asking, in effect:
“What am I willing to give?”
Jesus did not love His church by defending His convenience.
He gave Himself.

That does not mean your spouse gets unlimited control over your friendships, your phone, or your life. Scripture should never be twisted into justification for coercion, isolation, jealousy, surveillance, or abuse.
But neither should “You’re just insecure” become an automatic weapon for dismissing a spouse’s legitimate pain.
Imagine your husband or wife saying quietly:
“This relationship makes me uncomfortable.”
And your immediate response is:
“You need to trust me.”
Perhaps they do.
But another question deserves to be asked.
Why is maintaining access to your ex more important than addressing the heart of the person you vowed to love?
That does not automatically mean you must delete someone whenever your spouse feels uncomfortable. Couples need wisdom, honesty, context, and sometimes pastoral counsel.
But if removing an unnecessary connection would cost you almost nothing and bring genuine peace to your marriage, why does surrendering it feel so expensive?
Sometimes our resistance reveals more than the connection itself.
“I haven’t done anything.”
Maybe you haven’t.
Thank God.
But faithfulness is bigger than proving you have not committed adultery.
Jesus takes sexual purity into the interior life in Matthew 5:27–30. He confronts lust at the level of the heart and then uses deliberately severe imagery about removing what causes one to stumble.
Jesus is not commanding bodily mutilation. His shocking language emphasizes the seriousness with which disciples should treat sin.
In other words:
Do not pet what you should flee.
Do not feed what you should starve.
Do not preserve convenient access to something you already know repeatedly pulls your heart away from faithfulness.
There are marriages that did not collapse in a hotel room.
They began collapsing much earlier.
A notification.
A private joke.
A reaction to a story.
“How have you been?”
“I’ve been thinking about you.”
“Do you ever wonder what would have happened if…?”
Then deleting messages.
Turning the phone over.
Changing passwords.
Calling emotional intimacy “catching up.”
And by the time bodies cross a boundary, hearts may have been trespassing for months.
But hear this carefully:
This article is not accusing everyone who follows an ex of secretly wanting an affair.
That would be unfair.
The issue is not paranoia.
The issue is wisdom.
For some married couples, an ex remaining somewhere on a friends list genuinely carries no emotional significance whatsoever.
For others, it is gasoline sitting beside a fire nobody believes will spread.
Only you, your spouse, and ultimately God know which situation you are dealing with.
And God sees what nobody scrolling your profile can see.
He sees whether you search their name.
He sees whether you wait for their reaction.
He sees whether you compare your spouse with them.
He sees whether you revisit photographs.
He sees the conversation you deleted.
He sees the fantasy you immediately pushed away.
He sees the fantasy you did not push away.
He sees the wounded part of you that still wants an old person to regret losing you.
He sees everything.
And remarkably, the Gospel does not end there.
Because Jesus did not come merely to expose hidden rooms.
He came to redeem the people hiding inside them.
Maybe you have already crossed a line.
Maybe this article is no longer theoretical for you.
Maybe you kept the ex.
Then came the message.
Then another.
Maybe you told yourself your spouse would misunderstand, so you hid it.
Maybe emotional intimacy formed.
Maybe sexual conversation happened.
Maybe photographs were exchanged.
Maybe you met.
Maybe adultery happened.
And now you are reading this with your stomach tightening because this stopped being an article about social media several paragraphs ago.
Now it is about you.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But Jesus Christ is greater than your scandal.
The answer is not better hiding.
The answer is repentance.
Confession.
Truth.
Turning away from sin and toward Christ.
The Gospel does not say your betrayal was insignificant.
The Gospel says Christ's blood is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
At the cross, Jesus does something human beings could never accomplish for themselves.
He bears sin.
He offers forgiveness.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
He gives new life.
Grace does not rename adultery as harmless.
Grace takes guilty people who repent and begins rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
That is the difference between cheap permission and costly grace.
Cheap permission whispers:
“Everybody does it. Hide it better.”
Jesus says:
“Come into the light.”
Maybe your next act of worship is unfollowing somebody.
Maybe it is blocking somebody.
Maybe it is showing your spouse a conversation you have hidden.
Maybe it is ending emotional dependence on someone who does not belong in the intimate space of your marriage.
Maybe it is admitting you still carry feelings from a previous relationship and getting mature pastoral or professional help rather than pretending they do not exist.
Maybe the problem is not an ex at all.
Maybe the problem is your own jealousy, and Christ needs to heal your fear rather than requiring your spouse to spend a lifetime proving innocence.
Wisdom looks different in different circumstances.
But secrecy should always concern us.
If you would panic if your spouse picked up your phone…
If you repeatedly delete conversations…
If you speak to an ex about marital problems you refuse to discuss honestly with your spouse…
If you seek emotional affirmation from an ex…
If you fantasize about being with them…
If you hide the frequency or tone of your communication…
If their attention gives you something you should be cultivating within your marriage…
You are no longer dealing with an innocent question about a friends list.
Something needs to come into the light.
And maybe you are the spouse on the other side.
You saw the name.
You noticed the messages.
You felt foolish for being bothered.
You wondered whether speaking up would make you look controlling.
You tried to convince yourself it meant nothing.
Please remember this too:
Biblical love does not require pretending pain does not exist.
Speak truthfully.
Do not retaliate.
Do not manipulate.
Do not publicly humiliate your spouse.
Do not manufacture evidence.
Do not make accusations you cannot support.
But do not build peace on pretending.
Healthy marriages need truth.
And truth can hurt before it heals.
So should married people keep their exes on social media?
There is no universal biblical command requiring every married Christian to delete every ex.
But there is a universal call to holiness, wisdom, love, truth, purity, and faithfulness.
Therefore, ask better questions.
Does this connection strengthen my marriage or quietly weaken it?
Would I behave exactly the same way if my spouse were sitting beside me?
Am I protecting this connection because it is necessary—or because I enjoy what it gives me?
Would I be comfortable if my spouse interacted with their ex exactly as I interact with mine?
Is there secrecy?
Is there nostalgia becoming fantasy?
Is my spouse's concern reasonable?
Does keeping this person near help me become more faithful to Jesus?
And perhaps the hardest:
If Christ asked me to surrender this connection for the good of my marriage, why would I hesitate?
Marriage is already difficult enough without keeping unnecessary ghosts seated at the table.
Your spouse should not have to compete with a memory.
Your marriage should not have to survive a relationship you refuse to bury.
And you do not need to prove spiritual maturity by standing unnecessarily close to temptation.
Sometimes maturity looks remarkably unimpressive.
Unfollow.
Delete.
Block.
Tell the truth.
Put the phone down.
Turn toward your spouse.
Pray together.
Get help.
Forgive where repentance is real.
Rebuild what secrecy damaged.
And when necessary, establish boundaries strong enough that tomorrow's weakness cannot easily undo today's conviction.
But above everything else…
Turn toward Jesus.
Because you can delete every ex and still possess an unfaithful heart.
You can have perfect social-media boundaries and still be proud, lustful, selfish, bitter, dishonest, or emotionally absent.
Christianity is not behavior modification with Bible verses attached.
We need Christ.
We need His forgiveness.
We need His Spirit transforming our desires.
We need the Savior who does not merely clean our profile but changes our hearts.
And perhaps that is why this subject matters far beyond Facebook.
Sooner or later every disciple encounters something that forces the question:
Do I want Jesus only when He comforts me…
or is He Lord when obedience costs me something?
Be honest before God first. Then, if it reflects where you truly are, comment, “no more hiding.”
If your marriage has been fighting through wounds, temptation, mistrust, or restoration, comment, “Christ is still healing us.”
If you are struggling and need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, forgiveness, wise boundaries, patient rebuilding, and the grace of Christ can still write another chapter.
Not because every sentence applies to every marriage, but because there may come a night when you need to remember the question:
“Is this worth risking what God has entrusted to me?”
Not because God needs your money.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by financial support.
But if God has given you the ability and desire to support Gospel-centered work, voluntary generosity can itself be offered for His glory.
Give Jesus the room you keep locking.
Give Him the conversation.
Give Him the temptation.
Give Him the nostalgia.
Give Him the marriage.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the secret.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where biblical forgiveness is needed.
Seek wisdom where the situation is complicated.
And remember this:
Some doors need to close not because you still love the person behind them, but because you finally understand the value of the person God has placed beside you.
